items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to synchronization of multiple prescriptions
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5622

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to
synchronization of multiple prescriptions

 PURPOSE :

This bill provides for the synchronization of multiple prescriptions
for Medicaid recipients so that a beneficiary can pick up prescription
refills on the same day of each month.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Sections 1 and 2 amend Social Services law § 367-a(9) and § 364-j(4)
respectively to provide for the creation of a voluntary program for
medication synchronization of medications when it is agreed among the
member, a provider, and a pharmacists that synchronization of multiple
prescriptions for the treatment of a chronic illness is in the best
interest of the patient given certain conditions. Drug coverage shall
not be denied for a partial fill for any drug prescribed when it is
for the purposes of synchronization. To permit synchronization, an
individual or plan would allow a pharmacy to override any denial codes
indicating that a prescription is being refilled too soon, for the
purposes of medication synchronization.

Amendments also ensure a pro-rated cost-sharing rate shall be
permitted and applied to prescriptions that are dispensed for less
than a 30 day supply for the purpose of synchronizing the covered
individual's medications, and that the dispensing fee stays whole for
the pharmacist for a partial fill.

Section 3 sets the effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This bill would eliminate barriers to the implementation of medication
synchronization, a service that has been shown to improve the rates of
medication adherence and lower overall healthcare costs.

Medication synchronization refers to a voluntary program initiated by
a pharmacist in coordination with a physician and a beneficiary in
which the medication refills are coordinated so that every
prescription refill is due on the same day each month. The coordinated
timing of refills creates an opportunity for a meaningful dialogue
between a pharmacist and a patient about the goals of the medication
therapy, as well as problems with compliance and the strategies to
overcome or manage them.

It is estimated that 76% of Americans aged 60 and over use two or more
medicines and 37% take five or more. In fact, medication
synchronization was first studied in a clinical trial that
specifically addressed medication non adherence in the elderly. The
Federal Study of Adherence to Medications in the Elderly (FAME) was
conducted between June 2004 and August 2006. It involved 200 patients
65 years and older. FAME represents one of the few randomized
controlled studies to demonstrate improvement in both adherence and
health outcomes through a pharmacy program that used reminder
packaging in the form of blister packs. After six months of
pharmacists' intervention, medication adherence increased to 96.9%
from the baseline of 61.25% at the start of the study.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), the largest
payer for healthcare in the nation, implemented medication
synchronization as policy for Medicare Part D plans effective January
1, 2014. The Federal Register/Vol/77/April 12, 2012, estimates $1.8
billion in net savings (over 6 years) in Part D. Part D plans are
required to establish a daily cost-sharing rate to facilitate
pro-rated co-payments for prescriptions written for 30-day supplies,
which the pharmacist is dispensing in a smaller days' supply because
medications are being synchronized. One goal is to reduce waste from
unnecessary fills and ensure that beneficiaries receive only the
medication they need.

To date, 18 states have removed statutory and/or regulatory barriers
to medication synchronization through proactive legislation in
commercial plans. Importantly, legislation passed in Kentucky in 2015
and Ohio in 2016 gave Medicaid beneficiaries access to medication
synchronization.

Nothing in this bill requires medication synchronization. It simply
establishes a mechanism for medication synchronization for patients
with chronic illness when there is a voluntary agreed-upon plan
between the patient, the health care provider and the pharmacist.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New Bill

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the 120th day after becoming law.
